title: Traverse a binary tree: Inorder (Left -> Root -> Right gives sorted order in BST), Preorder (Root -> Left -> Right), Postorder (Left -> Right -> Root).
shortTitle: Traverse a Binary Tree (Inorder, Preorder, Postorder)

s1_definition.oneliner: Inorder visits left-node-right (sorted on BST), preorder visits node-left-right (clone/serialize), postorder visits left-right-node (delete/evaluate).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Inorder** – visit left subtree, then the node, then right subtree; produces sorted output on a BST.
- **Preorder** – visit the node first, then left, then right; used for cloning and serialisation.
- **Postorder** – visit left, then right, then the node last; used for deletion and expression evaluation.
- **Level-order** – visit nodes level by level using a queue; BFS traversal.
- **Complexity** – all traversals visit every node once, giving O(n) time and O(h) stack space for recursion.
s1_definition.analogy: Auditing the branch hierarchy at the National Bank of India requires different traversal orders for different reports. Inorder gives a sorted roster of account balances. Preorder gives a top-down export to replicate the hierarchy in a new branch. Postorder gives the safe shutdown order where every subordinate is closed before the manager.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Tree:        50
              /  \
            20    80
           /  \     \
         10    30    90

  Inorder  (L, N, R): 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 50 -> 80 -> 90  (sorted!)
  Preorder (N, L, R): 50 -> 20 -> 10 -> 30 -> 80 -> 90  (top-down)
  Postorder(L, R, N): 10 -> 30 -> 20 -> 90 -> 80 -> 50  (bottom-up)

  Traversal Template:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  void traverse(node):                       │
  │    if node == null: return                  │
  │    [PREORDER: visit(node)]                  │
  │    traverse(node.left)                      │
  │    [INORDER: visit(node)]                   │
  │    traverse(node.right)                     │
  │    [POSTORDER: visit(node)]                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Iterative Inorder (Stack):
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │ Push all lefts -> Pop -> Visit│
  │ -> Move to right -> Repeat   │
  └───────────────────────────────┘
  Stack: [50, 20, 10] -> pop 10 (visit) -> right=null
  Stack: [50, 20]     -> pop 20 (visit) -> right=30
  Stack: [50, 30]     -> pop 30 (visit) -> right=null
  Stack: [50]         -> pop 50 (visit) -> right=80
  ...
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Traversing a binary tree means visiting every node exactly once, and the three depth-first traversals differ only in when the current node is visited relative to its subtrees. Inorder visits left, then node, then right, and on a BST this produces sorted ascending output. Preorder visits the node first, then left, then right, making it the choice for cloning and serialisation. Postorder visits left, right, then node, making it the choice for safe deletion and expression evaluation.

The key interview insight is that each traversal order maps to a real use case. Inorder for sorted output, preorder for copy/serialize, postorder for teardown/evaluate, and level-order for breadth-first views. Being able to name the use case for each order shows understanding beyond memorisation.

At the National Bank of India, the product-approval hierarchy was stored as a tree. Inorder gave a sorted roster of approval amounts. Preorder gave a top-down export to replicate the hierarchy in a new branch. Postorder gave the safe decommissioning order. The same tree produced all three reports by changing only the position of the visit statement.

The senior-level nuances are the iterative versions and Morris traversal. Deep trees can overflow the call stack, so the iterative versions using an explicit stack handle any depth safely. Morris traversal achieves O(1) space by temporarily threading the tree, which matters in memory-constrained environments. Knowing that preorder plus inorder uniquely determines a binary tree is the basis of tree serialisation.

Remember one sentence: The three traversals differ only in the position of the visit statement relative to the recursive calls, and each order maps to a concrete use case: inorder for sorted output, preorder for cloning, postorder for deletion.

---

keyPoints: Inorder (L, N, R) produces sorted output on a BST.
Preorder (N, L, R) is used for cloning and serialisation.
Postorder (L, R, N) is used for safe deletion and expression evaluation.
All traversals are O(n) time and O(h) recursion stack space.
Iterative versions use an explicit stack to avoid stack overflow on deep trees.
Morris traversal achieves O(1) extra space by temporarily threading the tree.
